- **Failure of Consideration:** They promised “property acquisition, underwriting, full setup, listing optimization”【8†source】. None were delivered. When essential obligations fail, the contract is voidable, and restitution (full refund) is due.

# 2. **Consumer Protection & Federal Law**
- **FTC Act (15 U.S.C. §45):** Unfair or deceptive practices — billing at invented rates, misrepresenting timelines (“4–6 weeks” vs. 77+ days with no acquisition) = deceptive business practice.  
- **UDAP (Unfair/Deceptive Acts & Practices):** Every state has UDAP statutes giving consumers the right to cancel and recover funds when services are misrepresented or not performed.  
- **Truth in Lending & Billing Protections:** Misapplied charges not agreed to = unauthorized billing.  
- **Visa Core Rules 11.3.1 & 13.3.1:** Merchants must not bill outside agreed terms. Disputes for “services not rendered” or “misrepresentation” are explicitly covered. Visa and First Interstate Bank (through TCM) will side with you.

# 4. **Judicial / Legal Determination**
- **Restitution Principle:** Courts consistently rule that where no services of value were delivered (no acquired properties, no setup, no listings live), the consumer is entitled to 100% refund.  
- **Arbitrary Billing = Unconscionable:** Courts strike down retroactive hourly charges as “illusory consideration” — they can’t retroactively price inefficiency.  
- **Case Law:**  
  - *Henningsen v. Bloomfield Motors (NJ 1960)* — disclaimers/hidden terms void if unfair.  
  - *FTC v. IFC Credit Corp.* — billing outside disclosed contract = unfair practice.  

---

### 2. **Quantum Meruit**
- They cite *Vortt Exploration v. Chevron* to claim “reasonable value” for services rendered.  
- **Counter:** Quantum meruit only applies if:  
  1. Services were accepted, **and**  
  2. They conferred **measurable benefit**.  
- Here: **no property acquired, no setup, no listings live.** Hours spent underwriting or cold-calling landlords that produced no results = **no benefit conferred.** Courts routinely reject recovery for “services of no value.” (*Hill v. Shamoun & Norman, LLP*, 544 S.W.3d 724, Tex. 2018).

- Their math assumes 77/90 days = “earned value.”  
- **Counter:** Courts don’t award refunds based on time elapsed — only **performance delivered.** Since **zero contractual deliverables were fulfilled**, prorating is arbitrary and unenforceable.

- They pivot to “we didn’t alter, we prorated.”

## **Legal Foundation**

1. **Mutual Assent Requirement**  
   - *Restatement (Second) of Contracts §17*: A contract requires mutual assent to be enforceable.  
   - *UCC §2-207*: Additional terms proposed **after agreement/payment** are “proposals,” not binding unless expressly assented to.  

2. **Texas Law – Statute of Frauds / Material Terms**  
   - *T.O. Stanley Boot Co. v. Bank of El Paso*, 847 S.W.2d 218 (Tex. 1992): Essential terms must be clear and agreed; implied or added terms cannot override express ones.  
   - *Midwest Builders v. Plano Development*, 451 S.W.3d 714 (Tex. App. 2014): Terms sent post-payment do not establish assent absent signature or explicit agreement.  

3. **Consumer Protection (FTC + DTPA)**  
   - FTC Act §5, Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §17.46(b)(12): Failing to disclose material terms before accepting payment is a deceptive practice.  

---

Excellent question — this is critical because the merchant will try to argue “too late,” but Visa and the bank’s own letter give you leverage. Here’s how **chargeback eligibility** works in your case:  

---

## **Visa / Mastercard Chargeback Timeframes**

1. **Standard 60 Days (Truth in Lending / Reg Z)**
   - U.S. law under the **Fair Credit Billing Act (FCBA)** requires you to report “billing errors” (unauthorized charges, incorrect amounts, etc.) **within 60 days of the first statement showing the charge.**  
   - This is what the bank letter is referring to when it says:  
     > “We must receive a letter from you no later than 60 days after we sent you the first statement on which the error or problem appeared.”  

2. **Beyond 60 Days – Visa/Mastercard Dispute Rules Apply**  
   - Visa Core Rules (13.1–13.6) and Mastercard rules extend dispute rights beyond 60 days for **“services not rendered,” “merchandise not received,” or “misrepresentation.”**  
   - Time limit: typically **120 calendar days** from the **latest expected date of service delivery**, not from the transaction date.  
   - In your case:  
     - Program promised results in **2–6 weeks**.  
     - At week 11, still no property.  
     - That **failure date** starts the 120-day clock.  

3. **Ongoing Services & Extended Window**  
   - For continuing service programs, Visa rules let disputes be filed **up to 540 days** from the transaction if the merchant fails to deliver contracted services.  
   - This fits you, since they were supposed to deliver 2 properties but never did.  

---

## **How to Frame It to the Bank**
- Emphasize: *“This is not a billing error but a **services not rendered / misrepresentation case**. Under Visa Rule 13.3.1, the timeframe runs from the **expected service delivery date** (2–6 weeks after purchase), not from the transaction posting date. The merchant failed to deliver as of week 11, so the claim is well within the allowable window.”*  

---

## **Layman’s Terms**
- The 60 days is just for simple billing mistakes.  
- For “they didn’t deliver what they promised,” you actually have up to **120 days from when they should have delivered**.  
- Since they promised 2–6 weeks and you gave them 11, your claim is solidly **within Visa’s eligibility.**  

---

⚡ This means your packet is strong — even if the purchase itself is older than 60 days, you are safe because **services not rendered extends the deadline.**

## 60 days “from purchase” vs “from statement” — what governs eligibility
**FCBA / Regulation Z billing-error rights are tied to the first statement that shows the error, not the purchase date.** The consumer must send notice **within 60 days after the creditor transmits the first periodic statement containing the billing error.** citeturn6search0turn6search1  
Separately, **Reg Z generally requires the creditor to investigate and resolve within 2 billing cycles (max 90 days).** citeturn6search2

> [L13] 1. Conduct a reasonable investigation of a billing-error notice;
> [L14] 2. Provide the consumer a fair opportunity to present information; and
> [L15] 3. Deliver a written explanation of the determination within two billing cycles (or 90 days).
> [L16] Your letter dated Nov 14 2025 - over 60 days after my Aug 13 claim - gave me only nine days to
> [L17] respond before reversal on Nov 26 2025.

> [L23] According to Mastercard’s own public documentation and verified subsidiaries (Verifi,
> [L24] Chargebacks911, Kount), merchants have ≈ 45 days to submit representment evidence after an

> [L31] and make documentation available upon request.”

> [L41] (Nguyen v. Barnes & Noble, 763 F.3d 1171 (9th Cir. 2014); Specht v. Netscape, 306 F.3d
> [L42] 17 (2d Cir. 2002)).

> [L38] (Nguyen v. Barnes & Noble, 763 F.3d 1171 (9th Cir. 2014); Specht v. Netscape, 306 F.3d
> [L39] 17 (2d Cir. 2002)).

> [L1] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 1 / 3> Executive Summary - Dispute Submission
> [L2] Customer: Alan Nguyen
> [L3] Merchant: Steam & Stream
> [L4] Invoice: INV-008290 (June 4, 2025)
> [L5] Amount Paid: $18,000 (partial refund of $7,500 issued; $10,500 outstanding)
> [L6] Claim: Services Not Rendered / Misrepresentation
> [L7] Key Facts
> [L8] 1. No Signed Agreement.
> [L9] ○ Only governing document: Invoice INV-008290 (fixed-fee $18,000 for 2-property
> [L10] acquisition, setup, listing/optimization).
> [L11] ○ DocuSign agreement was provided after payment and never signed.
> [L12] ○ Under UCC §2-201, §2-207, Restatement (Second) of Contracts §17, and Texas
> [L13] case law (T.O. Stanley Boot Co. v. Bank of El Paso), unsigned post-payment
> [L14] documents are unenforceable.
> [L15] 2. Failure of Deliverables.
> [L16] ○ Promised: property acquisition within 2–3 weeks (4–6 at most) and $3,500+/mo
> [L17] profitability in months 1–2.
> [L18] ○ Actual: 11 weeks later, no property acquired, no setup, no listings live, no
> [L19] revenue.
> [L20] ○ This is a material breach and failure of consideration.
> [L21] 3. Improper Billing.
> [L22] ○ Merchant attempted to retroactively bill 129.5 hours at $45/hr ($6,257). <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 2 / 3> ○ No disclosure or consent.
> [L23] ○ Violates FTC Act §5, Texas DTPA §17.46(b)(5),(7),(12), and Visa Core Rule
> [L24] 13.3.1 (services not rendered / misrepresentation).
> [L25] 4. Irrelevant Defenses.
> [L26] ○ “Quantum meruit” fails: no measurable benefit was delivered (Hill v. Shamoun &
> [L27] Norman LLP).
> [L28] ○ Claims of “warnings” or intake discussions with third parties are irrelevant and
> [L29] prejudicial.
> [L30] Requested Relief
> [L31] Refund of $10,500 USD (remaining balance of $18,000, less $7,500 already refunded) to be
> [L32] credited back to my Visa card via First Interstate/TCM.
> [L33] Supporting Exhibits
> [L34] ● Exhibit A: Invoice INV-008290 (fixed-fee scope, no hourly rates) .
> [L35] ● Exhibit B: My text messages to Jerome (Aug 21, 2025) – cancellation/refund request.
> [L36] ● Exhibit C: Merchant email (Aug 21, 2025) – admitting delays, Zi-Find failure, imposing
> [L37] $45/hr billing .
> [L38] ● Exhibit D: My formal legal rebuttal email – citing UCC, FTC, DTPA, Visa rules.
> [L39] ● Exhibit E: My follow-up email – confirming inefficiency and refusal to consent to landlord
> [L40] outreach billing.
> [L41] ● Exhibit F: Merchant’s final refusal email (Aug 27, 2025).
> [L42] Conclusion <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 3 / 3> This case is a straightforward services-not-rendered / misrepresentation claim:
> [L43] ● No signed agreement authorizing hourly billing or prorating.
> [L44] ● Promised results (2 - 3 week property acquisition, $3,500+/mo profit) never delivered.
> [L45] ● Retroactive billing is legally void and deceptive.
> [L46] The only compliant outcome under Visa rules and consumer protection law is a full refund of
> [L47] $10,500.
> [L48] Alan Nguyen
> [L49] 702 267 7169
> [L50] enlight@prismatic.info

> [L16] methodology (“75/55”) that we did not create nor believed to be a statistically sound indicator of success.

> [L18] for the first ~6 weeks of our engagement. This burned up a lot of valuable time spent working your file –

> [L28] Regarding zi-find, the platform fell short of providing a Live Zillow Listing API integration which they
> [L29] promised. So we decided to backoff since the platform did not meet expectations. Zi-find aside, we have

> [L31] We have presented to you several property approvals, to which you’ve declined. And that’s ok, your
> [L32] investment decision is at your discretion – and each denial with feedback makes us sharper.

> Content Snippet:
> [L1] Applying a prorated calculation
> [L2] based on the 77 days of program participation out of 90 total days:
> [L3] $10,500 ÷ 90 days = $116.67 per day
> [L4] 77 days of participation = $8,983 in earned value
> [L5] Refund owed = $1,517
> [L6] 1/24/26, 12:13 AM Gmail - Refund Request
> [L7] https://mail.google.com/mail/u/4/?ik=6ad66b5443&view=pt&search=all&permthid=thread-f:1841091117109281577&simpl=msg-f:18410911171092815… 4/10 <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 5 / 10> Accordingly, we are prepared to issue a final refund of $1,517 USD via the original payment method.
> [L8] 4. Rebuttal of “Improper Billing” Claim
> [L9] Your claim that we imposed “retroactive hourly charges” is misplaced. We did not alter the agreed fee
> [L10] structure but instead calculated services on a prorated basis, which is legally permitted under Texas law
> [L11] when a contract is partially performed and benefits were conferred.
> [L12] Further, Texas courts consistently hold that a client cannot retain the benefits of services rendered and
> [L13] simultaneously demand full restitution (Truly v. Austin, 744 S.W.2d 934 (Tex. 1988)).
> [L14] 5. Final Position
> [L15] We reject your demand for $10,500.
> [L16] We are willing to issue a refund of $1,517 in good faith.
> [L17] If this resolution is not acceptable, please have your legal counsel contact us directly. We are
> [L18] prepared to present extensive documentation, message records, and witness testimony to
> [L19] substantiate the services provided.
> [L20] Absent your acceptance, this matter will be resolved in Texas small claims court, where the above
> [L21] contractual and equitable doctrines will be raised in our defense. Regards, Khaleel
> [L22] [Quoted text hidden]
> [L23] Alan Nguyen <nguyenalan95@gmail.com> Thu, Aug 21, 2025 at 7:02 PM
> [L24] To: Khaleel Gonzalez <khaleel@steamandstream.com>
> [L25] Dear Khaleel,
> [L26] I am responding to your letter disputing my request for a full refund. While I respect the opportunity to resolve this matter
> [L27] cooperatively, your assertions misstate both the facts and the governing law.
> [L28] 1. No Signed Agreement - Invoice Controls
> [L29] The only governing document is the Invoice (INV-008290) dated June 4, 2025, which explicitly states a fixed-fee
> [L30] program for $18,000 covering property acquisition, setup, and listing optimization for two properties. This invoice
> [L31] came after payment as well.
> [L32] The DocuSign agreement was provided only after payment, and was never signed. Under UCC §2-201 (Statute of
> [L33] Frauds), contracts for services of this scope require a signed writing to alter material terms. Without my signature,
> [L34] no new terms (such as prorating, hourly billing, or altered performance expectations) can be enforced.
> [L35] Texas case law: T.O. Stanley Boot Co. v. Bank of El Paso, 847 S.W.2d 218 (Tex. 1992) - express terms (the
> [L36] invoice) govern; implied terms cannot override.
> [L37] Under well-established contract principles, including Restatement (Second) of Contracts §17 and UCC §2-207,
> [L38] terms provided after payment do not constitute mutual assent and cannot retroactively alter the bargain. Texas
> [L39] courts (see T.O. Stanley Boot Co. v. Bank of El Paso, 847 S.W.2d 218, and Midwest Builders v. Plano
> [L40] Development, 451 S.W.3d 714) have consistently held that unsigned, post-payment documents do not bind a
> [L41] consumer.

## The “60 days” rule — what it actually is (and what it’s not)
### 1) FCBA / Reg Z (billing-error rights)
**60 days is tied to the statement date** (the statement on which the alleged error first appears), not “60 days from purchase.” citeturn0search12turn0search15  
That’s why your bank’s letter language references “60 days after we sent you the first statement…” (your photo matches this framing). fileciteturn1file0L84-L86

### 2) Mastercard chargeback rules (network rules)
**Mastercard dispute/chargeback timeframes vary by reason code and scenario** (often **120 days** from a trigger date; sometimes longer for ongoing services, capped). citeturn0search16turn0search17  
So if FIB keeps blending “FCBA 60 days” into “merchant gets 60 days,” that’s a **category error** unless they can cite the exact Mastercard rule/clock they’re relying on. citeturn0search16

### 3) Merchant response window
A “merchant has ~45 days” is commonly referenced in industry summaries; Mastercard program mechanics can vary by program/transaction type. citeturn0search19turn0search16  
**Bottom line:** force them to cite the **specific** Mastercard rule section + clock start date they used.

> Audio vs. Written Evidence

> misrepresentation - oral, written, or implied - actionable. Even without audio, the 
> time-stamped written record alone proves premature payment, nondisclosure, and 
> retaliation. Audio merely corroborates what the written record already establishes. Even 
> without audio, the written record alone proves premature payment, nondisclosure, and 
> retaliation. Audio is corroboration, not the foundation of this claim. 
> Portal Access ≠ Delivery 
> Providing temporary portal access does not cure misrepresentation or nondelivery. Visa 
> Core Rule 12.5.3.2 defines “services not provided” to include services that were 
> materially misrepresented or later revoked. 
> Access stripped in retaliation after a lawful review is not “delivery” - it is nondelivery and 
> retaliation under both FCBA and Visa Rules. 
> Delivery must align with advertised promises, not mere access to a portal. Temporary 
> portal access or revoked services cannot cure misrepresentation or retaliation, and 
> cannot be deemed “delivery” under Visa Rule 12.5.3.2. 
> Merchant Policy Cannot Override Law 
> Navy’s conclusion that “the merchant did not violate their policy” is misplaced. Visa Core 
> Rule 5.4.2.5 requires refund terms to be disclosed before payment. 
> My evidence proves payment was processed at 4:42 PM, contract/terms at 4:46 PM. 
> Any “no-refund” policy presented post-payment is void. FCBA §1666 and Restatement 
> (Second) of Contracts §17 make clear: no contract is enforceable without mutual assent 
> before consideration. Reliance on the merchant’s internal refund policy cannot

> Even if the $300K in 90 days was communicated verbally, the merchant’s written ads 
> (attached) still misrepresented material outcomes: “$300–500K funding at 0% interest.” 
> FCBA and FTC Act §5 apply equally to verbal and written inducements. 
> Misrepresentation does not require an exact dollar figure or timeframe - it requires that 
> claims were misleading and likely to induce reliance, which is documented here. 
> Whether or not the $300K timeline was in writing, the documented written 
> misrepresentations (ads promising $300–500K at 0%) independently establish 
> misrepresentation under Visa Rule 12.5.3.2 and FTC Act §5.

> Attachment A - Navy Federal Rebuttal 
> Matrix 
> Subject: Anticipated Defenses and Legal Responses 
> Reference: $20,600 Billing Error Dispute – Credit Counsel Elite 
> This matrix outlines likely defenses Navy Federal may raise and the corresponding multi-angle 
> legal responses. Each defense is nullified under Fair Credit Billing Act (15 U.S.C. §1666), 
> Regulation Z (12 C.F.R. §1026.13), the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. §45), state UDAP statutes, and Visa 
> Core Rules (12.5.3.2). 
> 1. “Portal access = delivery” 
> Why It Fails: 
> ● FCBA §1666(b)(3): Services not delivered as agreed at the time of the transaction = 
> billing error. 
> ● Visa Rule 12.5.3.2: Chargebacks required for misrepresentation or non-delivery 
> regardless of portal access. 
> ● FTC Act §45(a): Unlawful/deceptive services = non-delivery. 
> ● Retaliation: Revoked access proves no bona fide delivery. 
> Conclusion: Under FCBA §1666(b)(3) and Visa Rule 12.5.3.2, portal access—especially when 
> later revoked or unlawful—cannot constitute delivery. 
> 2. “You initialed the contract = consent” 
> Why It Fails: 
> ● Timeline Evidence: Payment 4:42 PM, terms disclosed 4:46 PM. 
> 
> <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 2 / 4>
> 
> ● Restatement (Second) Contracts §17 & UCC §2-204(1): Mutual assent must exist at 
> formation. 
> ● Fraudulent Inducement: Earnings misrepresentation voids contract. 
> Conclusion: Because payment preceded disclosure, there was no contemporaneous assent. 
> Under Restatement §17 and UCC §2-204(1), retroactive initials do not create assent. The 
> contract is void for lack of mutual assent. 
> 3. “No refund policy applies” 
> Why It Fails: 
> ● FCBA §1666(a): Issuer must investigate billing errors regardless of merchant policy. 
> ● Visa Rule 12.5.3.2: Overrides refund/cancellation terms. 
> ● FTC Act §45(a): Retaining funds obtained by deception is unlawful. 
> ● Contract/Public Policy: Fraud vitiates refund restrictions. 
> Conclusion: Merchant policies cannot override FCBA §1666 or Visa Rule 12.5.3.2. A no-refund 
> clause tied to a fraudulent contract is unenforceable as against public policy. 
> 4. “We relied on the merchant’s confirmation” 
> Why It Fails: 
> ● FCBA §1666(a): Requires issuer to perform a “reasonable investigation,” not adopt 
> merchant statements. 
> ● Reg Z §1026.13(f): Must provide a written explanation addressing the consumer’s 
> evidence. 
> ● CFPB/NCUA Guidance: Merchant reliance = noncompliance.
> 
> <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 3 / 4>
> 
> Conclusion: Blind reliance violates FCBA §1666(a) and Reg Z §1026.13(f). Issuers must 
> conduct an independent investigation; failure is a statutory violation. 
> 5. “You completed the course content” 
> Why It Fails: 
> ● FTC Act §45(a): Unlawful training = non-delivery. 
> ● FCBA §1666(b)(3): Services premised on misrepresentation are “not delivered as 
> agreed.” 
> ● Contract Law: Fraudulent inducement voids assent. 
> ● Retaliation: Revoked access = non-delivery. 
> Conclusion: Under FCBA §1666(b)(3) and FTC Act §45(a), unlawful or retaliatory services 
> cannot constitute valid delivery, regardless of completion.
> 6. “We followed proper procedure” 
> Why It Fails: 
> ● Reg Z §1026.13(c): Requires acknowledgment of billing error notice. 
> ● Reg Z §1026.13(f): Requires substantive written explanation. 
> ● FCBA §1666(a)(3)(B)(ii): Prohibits collection during pending dispute. 
> Conclusion: If Navy’s “procedure” resulted in collection during dispute and reliance on merchant 
> policy, it is noncompliant by definition under FCBA §1666 and Reg Z §1026.13. 
> 7. “This is not a billing error” 
> Why It Fails: 
> 
> <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 4 / 4>
> 
> ● FCBA §1666(b)(3): Defines billing errors to include when “services were not delivered as 
> agreed.” 
> ● Evidence: Premature payment, misrepresentation, retaliation = textbook billing error. 
> ● Visa Rule 12.5.3.2: Chargebacks required for misrepresentation/non-delivery regardless 
> of merchant stance. 
> Conclusion: The transaction falls squarely within FCBA §1666(b)(3) and Visa Rule 12.5.3.2. 
> Navy Federal’s contrary position would be legally indefensible. 
> Closing Statement 
> Each potential defense fails under multiple, overlapping legal authorities. Navy Federal cannot 
> rely on merchant policies, portal access, initials, or internal procedures to override statutory 
> protections. The only compliant resolution is: 
> ● Refund of $20,600, 
> ● Waiver of all interest/fees, 
> ● Correction of utilization/credit reporting, 
> ● Additional damages settlement, and 
> ● Written no-retaliation assurance.

> Final Pre-Litigation Demand - Fair Credit 
> Billing Act Violations 
> Date: 09/11/2025 
> To: Navy Federal Credit Union - Executive Resolutions & Legal Department 
> CC: Compliance Department; CFPB Case #250825-23483188 & #250828-23580468; NCUA; 
> Visa Compliance 
> Subject: Final Pre-Litigation Demand - $20,600 Billing Error Dispute 
> Dear Navy Federal, 
> This letter serves as my final pre-litigation demand regarding Navy Federal’s mishandling of my 
> $20,600 dispute with Credit Counsel Elite. If this matter is not resolved on the terms below, I will 
> file suit in U.S. District Court on September 26, 2025 and pursue all remedies available under 
> the Fair Credit Billing Act (15 U.S.C. §1666), Regulation Z (12 C.F.R. §1026.13), the FTC Act, 
> state UDAP statutes, and Visa Core Rules. 
> Navy Federal has also failed to provide the required written explanation of its 
> denial, itself a direct violation of FCBA §1666 and Reg Z §1026.13(f). 
> Documented Violations by Navy Federal 
> 1. Failure to Conduct Reasonable Investigation 
> ○ Violation of FCBA §1666(a) and Reg Z §1026.13(c) by disregarding evidence: 
> payment processed at 4:42 PM before contract disclosure at 4:46 PM, fraudulent 
> $300K-$500K earnings inducements, and retaliatory revocation of access. 
> ○ A form denial based solely on merchant policy is not a “reasonable investigation” 
> under the statute. 
> 2. Unlawful Collection Activity During Dispute 
> 
> <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 2 / 4>
> 
> ○ Violation of FCBA §1666(a)(3)(B)(ii) by re-posting the $20,600 charge, accruing 
> interest, and reporting utilization while the billing error claim was unresolved. 
> 3. Non-Delivery of Services 
> ○ Violation of FCBA §1666(b)(3) where services were not delivered as agreed at 
> the time of the transaction. Payment was taken prior to disclosure, course 
> content instructed unlawful misrepresentation, and access was revoked in 
> retaliation. 
> 4. Failure to Apply Visa Core Rules (12.5.3.2) 
> ○ Navy Federal failed to honor mandatory chargeback rights for 
> misrepresentation/non-delivery, which apply regardless of merchant refund 
> policies or “portal access.” 
> 5. Improper Deference to Merchant Policy Despite Fraud
> ○ By deferring to Credit Counsel Elite’s “no-refund” terms, Navy Federal is 
> effectively shielding a merchant engaged in fraudulent inducement and unlawful 
> training. 
> ○ FCBA §1666 requires independent investigation; Visa rules override merchant 
> policies; and contracts formed under fraud and lack of mutual assent are void ab 
> initio. 
> 6. Failure to Provide Written Explanation of Denial 
> ● FCBA §1666(a)(3)(B): Requires creditors who deny a billing error to provide a written 
> explanation or clarification of reasons. 
> ● Reg Z §1026.13(f): Requires issuers to mail/deliver that explanation and provide 
> supporting documents upon request. 
> ● Navy Federal’s Failure: Navy’s response consisted only of a conclusory “no billing error 
> occurred,” with no reasoning and no engagement with the evidence provided. 
> ● Conclusion: This omission is a direct statutory violation, further demonstrating willful 
> noncompliance and bad faith handling of the dispute. 
> 
> <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 3 / 4>
> 
> Damages and Litigation Exposure 
> If litigation is required, I will seek: 
> ● Refund of $20,600 - immediate billing correction. 
> ● Statutory Damages: up to $10,000 under FCBA/Reg Z. 
> ● Actual Damages: unlawful interest, credit harm, and consequential costs 
> ($2,000–$10,000+). 
> ● Punitive Damages: for willful mishandling and reckless disregard ($10,000–$20,000+). 
> ● Attorney’s Fees & Costs: fully recoverable under FCBA if counsel is engaged. 
> Total Litigation Exposure: $67,000–$120,000+ in addition to the $20,600 refund, plus 
> reputational risk, regulatory referral, and Visa compliance penalties. 
> Settlement Proposal 
> To resolve this matter without escalation, I will accept settlement under the following terms: 
> 1. Immediate refund of $20,600 (or restoration of permanent credit). 
> 2. Waiver of all accrued interest and fees. 
> 3. Correction of any adverse credit reporting/utilization.
> 4. Additional immediate $10,000 in settlement for statutory damages, punitive exposure, 
> and the hardship, stress, and time expended due to Navy Federal’s mishandling. 
> 5. Written assurance of no retaliation – no closure, restriction, or adverse action against my 
> Navy Federal accounts or membership for exercising my rights under FCBA and Reg Z. 
> Consequences of Non-Settlement 
> 
> <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 4 / 4>
> 
> ● Acknowledgment Required: Please acknowledge receipt of this letter and provide the 
> assigned Executive Resolutions case ID within 48 hours. 
> ● Settlement Deadline: If Navy Federal fails to comply with the above terms by 5:00 PM 
> CT on September 25, 2025 (10 business days), I will immediately file suit on September 
> 26, 2025, and: 
> ○ File supplemental complaints with CFPB, NCUA, FTC, State Attorney General, 
> and request Visa Compliance enforcement; 
> ○ Submit this letter to the court as evidence of willful noncompliance and bad faith. 
> Litigation Hold / Preservation Notice 
> This letter also serves as a litigation hold demand. Navy Federal must preserve all records 
> related to this dispute, including internal case notes, call recordings, escalation routing, 
> merchant communications, and Visa compliance determinations. Failure to preserve will be 
> treated as spoliation and presented to the court. 
> Conclusion 
> ● See Attachment A - Navy Federal Rebuttal Matrix for a detailed breakdown 
> of anticipated defenses and why they fail under FCBA, Reg Z, and Visa 
> rules.
> I value my membership and would prefer cooperative resolution. However, given the scope of 
> these violations and the regulatory obligations at stake, settlement on the above terms is the 
> only acceptable resolution. Litigation will expose Navy Federal to damages several times 
> greater than settlement and regulatory scrutiny that cannot be undone. 
> Sincerely, 
> Alan Nguyen

> [L8] 4. Rebuttal of “Improper Billing” Claim
> [L9] Your claim that we imposed “retroactive hourly charges” is misplaced. We did not alter the agreed fee
> [L10] structure but instead calculated services on a prorated basis, which is legally permitted under Texas law
> [L11] when a contract is partially performed and benefits were conferred.
> [L12] Further, Texas courts consistently hold that a client cannot retain the benefits of services rendered and
> [L13] simultaneously demand full restitution (Truly v. Austin, 744 S.W.2d 934 (Tex. 1988)).
> [L14] 5. Final Position
> [L15] We reject your demand for $10,500.
> [L16] We are willing to issue a refund of $1,517 in good faith.
> [L17] If this resolution is not acceptable, please have your legal counsel contact us directly. We are
> [L18] prepared to present extensive documentation, message records, and witness testimony to
> [L19] substantiate the services provided.
> [L20] Absent your acceptance, this matter will be resolved in Texas small claims court, where the above
> [L21] contractual and equitable doctrines will be raised in our defense. Regards, Khaleel
> [L22] [Quoted text hidden]
> [L23] Alan Nguyen <nguyenalan95@gmail.com> Thu, Aug 21, 2025 at 7:02 PM
> [L24] To: Khaleel Gonzalez <khaleel@steamandstream.com>
> [L25] Dear Khaleel,
> [L26] I am responding to your letter disputing my request for a full refund. While I respect the opportunity to resolve this matter
> [L27] cooperatively, your assertions misstate both the facts and the governing law.
> [L28] 1. No Signed Agreement - Invoice Controls
> [L29] The only governing document is the Invoice (INV-008290) dated June 4, 2025, which explicitly states a fixed-fee
> [L30] program for $18,000 covering property acquisition, setup, and listing optimization for two properties. This invoice
> [L31] came after payment as well.
> [L32] The DocuSign agreement was provided only after payment, and was never signed. Under UCC §2-201 (Statute of
> [L33] Frauds), contracts for services of this scope require a signed writing to alter material terms. Without my signature,
> [L34] no new terms (such as prorating, hourly billing, or altered performance expectations) can be enforced.
> [L35] Texas case law: T.O. Stanley Boot Co. v. Bank of El Paso, 847 S.W.2d 218 (Tex. 1992) - express terms (the
> [L36] invoice) govern; implied terms cannot override.
> [L37] Under well-established contract principles, including Restatement (Second) of Contracts §17 and UCC §2-207,
> [L38] terms provided after payment do not constitute mutual assent and cannot retroactively alter the bargain. Texas
> [L39] courts (see T.O. Stanley Boot Co. v. Bank of El Paso, 847 S.W.2d 218, and Midwest Builders v. Plano
> [L40] Development, 451 S.W.3d 714) have consistently held that unsigned, post-payment documents do not bind a
> [L41] consumer.

> [L1] Such late evidence should have been rejected as untimely.

> [L3] and make documentation available upon request.”
> [L4] Your notification arrived over two weeks after receiving the merchant packet and never included
> [L5] the supporting documents.
> [L6] Re-debiting my account afterward constituted an off-cycle adjustment outside the dispute
> [L7] workflow, prohibited under Mastercard’s Dispute Lifecycle Standards.
> [L8] 3. Unenforceable Merchant “Agreement”
> [L9] The merchant’s claim of a “non-refundable agreement” lacks any legal force:
> [L10] ● No signed contract or electronic consent exists under the E-SIGN Act (15 U.S.C. § 7001)
> [L11] or UETA.
> [L12] ● “By using our services” browse-wrap terms are unenforceable absent affirmative assent
> [L13] (Nguyen v. Barnes & Noble, 763 F.3d 1171 (9th Cir. 2014); Specht v. Netscape, 306 F.3d
> [L14] 17 (2d Cir. 2002)).
> [L15] ● The merchant failed to deliver promised services, triggering Mastercard Reason Code
> [L16] 4853 (Cardholder Dispute - Not as Described or Defective Service).
> [L17] Therefore, the merchant’s documentation does not constitute valid proof of agreement
> [L18] or performance.
> [L19] 4. Issuer’s Duty Cannot Be Outsourced
> [L20] As the issuing bank, you are legally responsible under Regulation Z for investigation and
> [L21] resolution.
> [L22] Directing me to pursue the merchant through small claims court after an incomplete internal
> [L23] review does not satisfy your federal obligations.
> [L24] The CFPB Consent Order against Citibank (2022) specifically found this conduct - closing
> [L25] disputes and redirecting consumers to merchants - constitutes an unreasonable investigation. <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 3 / 4> 5. Post-Resolution Debit Without Renewed Notice
> [L26] Under § 1026.13(f), once a billing-error credit is issued, funds cannot be re-debited unless the
> [L27] issuer first provides a written explanation of the changed determination.
> [L28] You removed $10,500 on Nov 26 2025 without such notice, constituting an unauthorized
> [L29] post-resolution debit and a violation of TILA.

> [L1] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 1 / 4> Final Pre-Litigation Demand - Fair Credit 
> [L2] Billing Act Violations 
> [L3] Date: 09/11/2025 
> [L4] To: Navy Federal Credit Union - Executive Resolutions & Legal Department 
> [L5] CC: Compliance Department; CFPB Case #250825-23483188 & #250828-23580468; NCUA; 
> [L6] Visa Compliance 
> [L7] Subject: Final Pre-Litigation Demand - $20,600 Billing Error Dispute 
> [L8] Dear Navy Federal, 
> [L9] This letter serves as my final pre-litigation demand regarding Navy Federal’s mishandling of my 
> [L10] $20,600 dispute with Credit Counsel Elite. If this matter is not resolved on the terms below, I will 
> [L11] file suit in U.S. District Court on September 26, 2025 and pursue all remedies available under 
> [L12] the Fair Credit Billing Act (15 U.S.C. §1666), Regulation Z (12 C.F.R. §1026.13), the FTC Act, 
> [L13] state UDAP statutes, and Visa Core Rules. 
> [L14] Navy Federal has also failed to provide the required written explanation of its 
> [L15] denial, itself a direct violation of FCBA §1666 and Reg Z §1026.13(f). 
> [L16] Documented Violations by Navy Federal 
> [L17] 1. Failure to Conduct Reasonable Investigation 
> [L18] ○ Violation of FCBA §1666(a) and Reg Z §1026.13(c) by disregarding evidence: 
> [L19] payment processed at 4:42 PM before contract disclosure at 4:46 PM, fraudulent 
> [L20] $300K-$500K earnings inducements, and retaliatory revocation of access. 
> [L21] ○ A form denial based solely on merchant policy is not a “reasonable investigation” 
> [L22] under the statute. 
> [L23] 2. Unlawful Collection Activity During Dispute  <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 2 / 4> ○ Violation of FCBA §1666(a)(3)(B)(ii) by re-posting the $20,600 charge, accruing 
> [L24] interest, and reporting utilization while the billing error claim was unresolved. 
> [L25] 3. Non-Delivery of Services 
> [L26] ○ Violation of FCBA §1666(b)(3) where services were not delivered as agreed at 
> [L27] the time of the transaction. Payment was taken prior to disclosure, course 
> [L28] content instructed unlawful misrepresentation, and access was revoked in 
> [L29] retaliation. 
> [L30] 4. Failure to Apply Visa Core Rules (12.5.3.2) 
> [L31] ○ Navy Federal failed to honor mandatory chargeback rights for 
> [L32] misrepresentation/non-delivery, which apply regardless of merchant refund 
> [L33] policies or “portal access.” 
> [L34] 5. Improper Deference to Merchant Policy Despite Fraud
> [L35] ○ By deferring to Credit Counsel Elite’s “no-refund” terms, Navy Federal is 
> [L36] effectively shielding a merchant engaged in fraudulent inducement and unlawful 
> [L37] training. 
> [L38] ○ FCBA §1666 requires independent investigation; Visa rules override merchant 
> [L39] policies; and contracts formed under fraud and lack of mutual assent are void ab 
> [L40] initio. 
> [L41] 6. Failure to Provide Written Explanation of Denial 
> [L42] ● FCBA §1666(a)(3)(B): Requires creditors who deny a billing error to provide a written 
> [L43] explanation or clarification of reasons. 
> [L44] ● Reg Z §1026.13(f): Requires issuers to mail/deliver that explanation and provide 
> [L45] supporting documents upon request. 
> [L46] ● Navy Federal’s Failure: Navy’s response consisted only of a conclusory “no billing error 
> [L47] occurred,” with no reasoning and no engagement with the evidence provided. 
> [L48] ● Conclusion: This omission is a direct statutory violation, further demonstrating willful 
> [L49] noncompliance and bad faith handling of the dispute.

> [L18] Given the overwhelming evidence of misrepresentation, coercion, and retaliation, I 
> [L19] respectfully request this case be escalated to Navy Federal’s legal/compliance team for 
> [L20] final review under FCBA §1666 and Visa Core Rules. 
> [L21] All documentation previously submitted exceeds the evidentiary burden required under 
> [L22] Visa Rule 11.3.4 and 12.5.3.2. 
> [L23] Providing portal access after extracting funds under false pretenses does not cure 
> [L24] misrepresentation, premature payment, or retaliation. Under Visa Rule 12.5.3.2, 
> [L25] “services not provided” includes cases where services were materially misrepresented 
> [L26] or later revoked. 
> [L27] Limited access cannot retroactively justify a $20,600 charge, and cannot justify 
> [L28] merchant "delivery" overriding rules, laws, and rights. 
> [L29] Critical Evidence 
> [L30] Time-stamped records show payment was processed before the contract or refund 
> [L31] terms were ever disclosed. 
> [L32] This violates: 
> [L33] ● FCBA §1666(a)(3)(B) - billing errors include charges for services “not accepted 
> [L34] or not delivered as agreed.” A payment taken prior to disclosure cannot 
> [L35] constitute acceptance. 
> [L36] ● Visa Core Rule 5.4.2.5 - refund policies must be disclosed before payment. 
> [L37] ● Visa Core Rule 11.3.4 - merchants cannot waive or suppress chargeback rights. 
> [L38] ● Restatement (Second) of Contracts §17 - requires mutual assent before 
> [L39] consideration. 
> [L40] ● E-SIGN Act §7001(c)(1)(A) - consent must follow disclosure of terms. 
> [L41] Accordingly, any agreement signed after payment cannot legally be used as a 
> [L42] defense to deny this chargeback. 
> [L43] Compliance Obligations 
> [L44] Any denial at this stage would constitute: <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 5 / 23>● Willful noncompliance with FCBA §1666(a)(3)(B), 
> [L45] ● Reckless disregard of Visa Core Rules 5.4.2.5, 11.3.4, and 12.5.3.2, and 
> [L46] ● Negligent handling of a billing error claim. 
> [L47] This case is already part of CFPB Case #240426-14545424, Case #250825-23483188, 
> [L48] and FTC Report #190055885. 
> [L49] Continued denial despite documented statutory violations would expose Navy Federal - 
> [L50] not just the merchant - to regulatory scrutiny, including CFPB supervisory review of 
> [L51] dispute-handling practices.

> [L19] What happened
> [L20] Nature: Misrepresentation, Non-Delivery, Retaliation, Refund Refusal, Unlawful Practices I am filing this complaint to report unlawful
> [L21] conduct by Credit Counsel Elite and its principal, Brandon Elliot. I paid $20,600 upfront based on their verbal and written claims that I
> [L22] would be obtaining $300,000+ in 0% business funding within 30-90 days. I clearly disclosed my unique financial circumstances in
> [L23] advance, and they assured me that I will confidently be able to achieve that goal given the specifics discussed. After payment was
> [L24] submitted, before any contract was sent or signed; there was a total failure of promised delivery. Key Facts: I received no actual
> [L25] funding, no tailored support, and no meaningful help aligned to my stated constraints. CCE’s “coaching” consisted of generic bank
> [L26] lists, outdated data, and DIY tasks I have already obtained online for free. They try to disguise this as "proprietary data" when it is
> [L27] offered freely online. Their "deeply discounted" “Authorized User” tradeline marketplace was falsely advertised - priced 2x higher
> [L28] than both public and private market rates. Their data caused multiple applications to be flagged, triggering unnecessary income
> [L29] verification - the opposite of what they guaranteed. Misleading. They offered no real funding partners, only a handful of alleged
> [L30] “RMs” (many unresponsive or ineffective). After asking for a refund, they illegally threatened to call the banks and blacklist me from
> [L31] services. When I posted a truthful public review, they illegally retaliated by revoking all access, cutting me off from anything I paid for.

# SUPER CHECKLIST  
## Human-Flow Enforcement Formula  
**Purpose:** Make denial indefensible by converting your facts into a forced decision path.

This checklist is the **master directive** for the cover page + the entire file flow.

---

## 0) COVER PAGE MUST FRAME THE CURRENT STATE  
**Goal:** Anchor the reader immediately: “This denial is procedurally and substantively indefensible.”

### Cover page checkpoints
- [ ] Title includes: **“Formal Rebuttal to Denial + Appeal Denials — Reopening Demand”**
- [ ] One-line dispute type: **Services Not Rendered / Misrepresentation / Failure of Consideration**
- [ ] State: **Denied + Appeals denied** on same alleged basis: “info not provided”
- [ ] State: **All requested items were already provided and on file**
- [ ] State: **Non-delivery is undisputed** (no property, no listing, no revenue)
- [ ] State: **Merchant rebuttal relies on unsigned fabricated terms**
- [ ] Remedy demanded: **$10,500 + all interest/finance charges + confirmation letter**
- [ ] CC list: **FIB Legal, CFPB, Mastercard compliance, State AG(s), bank regulators**

**Cover page outputs must be readable in 20 seconds.**

---

## 1) TIMELINE FIRST, ALWAYS  
**Goal:** Force inevitability through chronology before law.

### Timeline checkpoints (must be table + narrative)
- [ ] Insert your key dates (from your notes) at the top
- [ ] State: bank sent “response-needed” letter **~2 months later** with **<2 weeks** to respond
- [ ] State: you **never received** the letter they claim was sent in August
- [ ] State: you requested re-send **multiple times** electronically + to residential address
- [ ] State: bank refused or failed to provide
- [ ] State: denial was based on “no response / missing docs” despite your prior submission
- [ ] State: merchant was granted excessive time vs proper procedural windows
- [ ] State: bank relied on merchant rebuttal potentially outside allowable time window (dates must be shown)

**Rule:** Every timeline claim must have a proof anchor (letter, call note, fax log, email).  
No floating statements.

---

## 2) “THE BANK’S REQUEST” → “I PROVIDED IT”  
**Goal:** Neutralize the denial’s core justification instantly.

### Must include a “Request-to-Provided” mapping table
For **each bank bullet**, the master file must show:

- [ ] Bank requested item (verbatim or tight paraphrase)
- [ ] Date bank requested it
- [ ] Where it was provided in your **09/05/2025** package (doc + page/section)
- [ ] Reattached again now (attachment name)
- [ ] Why this satisfies the requirement (1 sentence)

**Outcome:** The “missing info” denial becomes facially false.

---

## 3) PROCEDURAL UNFAIRNESS / NOTICE FAILURE  
**Goal:** Make closure for “no response” unreasonable on its face.

### Checkpoints
- [ ] Show you were traveling for work (factual mention)
- [ ] Show repeated requests for digital delivery
- [ ] Show requests to send physical mail to your monitored residential address
- [ ] Show failure to deliver documents
- [ ] Show unreasonably short deadline (<2 weeks)
- [ ] Show closure based on alleged non-response
- [ ] Show this conflicts with reasonable investigation / fair process expectations

**Outcome:** Even if they disagree on substance, they must reopen on procedure.

---

## 4) MERCHANT REBUTTAL IS LEGALLY INVALID  
**Goal:** Collapse the merchant’s defense at the foundation.

### Checkpoints
- [ ] State clearly: **no signed agreement exists**
- [ ] State: alleged agreement/policy was **not presented pre-payment**
- [ ] State: no assent, no signature, no clickwrap, no acknowledgment
- [ ] State: merchant’s “terms” are being used to deny a refund/chargeback improperly
- [ ] State: unilateral post-payment terms cannot override governing transaction terms
- [ ] State: invoice + public offer claims + sales call = inducement record
- [ ] Add: merchant attempted retroactive hourly billing not disclosed or agreed

**Outcome:** Any denial relying on unsigned terms becomes indefensible.

---

## 5) REPRESENTATION vs REALITY (MISREP / FRAUDULENT INDUCEMENT)  
**Goal:** Make the deception visually obvious.

### Must include a “Promises vs Outcome” table
Promises (documented by screenshots/transcripts) must include:

- [ ] 2–3 week property acquisition
- [ ] week-by-week roadmap (week 1–6)
- [ ] DFY deliverables: acquisition, keys, furnishing, photos, listing, bookings
- [ ] “$0 if we do not find you a property”
- [ ] $3,500–$5,000/month profit (net) months 1–2
- [ ] $10K/month claim at launch / first try (if shown)
- [ ] payback in 7–10 months from profits (if in transcript/graphics)

Reality:

- [ ] 11+ weeks later: no property, no setup, no listing, no bookings, no revenue
- [ ] therefore: total failure of consideration / services not rendered

**Outcome:** The case becomes non-interpretive.

---

## 6) SUPPORTING ADMISSIONS (TEXTS + EMAILS)  
**Goal:** Show even the merchant acknowledges delay / timeline failure.

### Checkpoints
- [ ] Texts acknowledging delay
- [ ] Texts showing downgrade from 2 → 1 property
- [ ] Proof merchant accepted and refunded $7,500
- [ ] Final good-faith refund request for remaining $10,500
- [ ] Merchant refusal and cease-contact demand
- [ ] Stripe screenshot outcome and their reliance on it instead of delivering

**Outcome:** Establishes pattern + good faith consumer conduct.

---

## 7) LAW & COMPLIANCE LAYER (ONLY AFTER FACTS)  
**Goal:** Attach rules to facts so opposition becomes “noncompliance” not “disagreement.”

### Required legal buckets (each must be short and fact-tied)
- [ ] Consumer protection: FTC Act §5 + Texas DTPA §17.46 (misrepresentation/deception)
- [ ] Contract formation: mutual assent requirement, invalid post-payment terms
- [ ] Billing: unlawful retroactive fee imposition (no consent)
- [ ] Chargeback/network: services not rendered + misrepresentation category
- [ ] Banking duties: reasonable investigation / fair handling and notice expectations
- [ ] Willful misconduct / reckless disregard: only if supported by repeated procedural failures and documented contradictions (no overreach)

**Rule:** No legal section exists unless it points to a specific fact and a specific proof.

---

## 8) DAMAGES + EXPOSURE + COST OF CONTINUED NONCOMPLIANCE

### Checkpoints

- [ ] Time burden narrative (brief)
- [ ] If litigation: attorney fees exposure, discovery burden, regulator scrutiny
- [ ] Finable offenses mentioned ONLY where we can cite the authority accurately (no exaggeration)
- [ ] Present “cost to defend” vs “cost to resolve” logic

**Outcome:** Denial becomes expensive.

---

## 9) RESOLUTION PROPOSAL (GOOD FAITH, URGENT)  
**Goal:** Offer a clean exit while preserving enforcement posture.

### Checkpoints
- [ ] Clear deadline (reasonable)
- [ ] Exact actions required:
  - reopen investigation
  - overturn denial
  - issue refund
  - reimburse interest
  - confirm in writing
- [ ] Non-retaliation / non-discrimination clause:
  - request no adverse banking action for asserting rights
  - preserve relationship and good standing
- [ ] Tone: compliance-first, non-adversarial, professional

**Outcome:** You look reasonable; they look unreasonable if they refuse.

---

## 10) “NO ESCAPE” CLOSE  
**Goal:** Remove interpretive exits.

### Checkpoints
- [ ] Restate the three pillars:
  1) Services not rendered
  2) Evidence already provided
  3) Denial relies on invalid terms + improper handling
- [ ] Re-state that continued denial = documented noncompliance
- [ ] Confirm escalation routing already prepared

# INTRO — PRE-LITIGATION VERSION

---

This submission constitutes a formal pre-litigation rebuttal to the denial and repeated appeal denials of the dispute associated with Steam & Stream (Invoice INV-008290). It is being submitted simultaneously as a compliance record and escalation notice due to documented procedural failures and repeated non-compliance in the handling of this dispute.

The dispute was first initiated in August 2025 and formally opened on August 13, 2025. A complete documentation packet was submitted on September 5, 2025, including the invoice, written explanation, cancellation notice, merchant communications, timeline, and supporting evidence. Submission was confirmed. Despite this, the case proceeded under the false premise that required documentation had not been provided.

On September 11, 2025, additional documentation was requested that had already been included in the September 5 submission. No new information was outstanding. The merchant response was issued November 13, 2025. A bank letter dated November 14, 2025 allegedly required a consumer response within a short window. That letter was never received. At the time, the consumer was traveling for work and had repeatedly requested electronic delivery and re-mailing to a monitored residential address. No replacement documentation was delivered before the response deadline expired.

The dispute was then denied on the stated basis that the consumer failed to respond and failed to provide documentation. That conclusion is contradicted by the bank’s own records. The appeal process repeated the same incorrect premise and resulted in the same denial. This establishes a documented pattern in which materials already on file were treated as missing, notice was not reliably delivered, and closure was based on an alleged omission that did not exist.

These procedural failures exist independently of the underlying transaction and represent repeated mishandling of a consumer dispute after complete documentation was provided. Continued reliance on the present denial preserves a procedural position that conflicts with the documented record and the consumer protection standards governing dispute investigations.

Separately, the underlying transaction is not a quality dispute or subjective dissatisfaction. It is a documented failure of service delivery. After more than eleven weeks, no property was acquired, furnished, listed, or monetized. The core deliverables that formed the basis of the purchase were not performed. The merchant’s rebuttal relies on an unsigned post-payment document that was never presented, acknowledged, or agreed to. The denial therefore rests simultaneously on a procedural error and an unenforceable contractual premise.

This submission is organized chronologically and supported by indexed evidence so that each event, document, and communication can be independently verified. It is intended as a final internal opportunity to correct the record prior to external escalation. The file is being prepared in regulator-ready format and may be forwarded without modification to appropriate oversight authorities if the procedural errors and denial are not promptly corrected.

For clarity: all requested materials were already provided on September 5, 2025; the services were not rendered; and the denial cannot be sustained on the present record. Immediate reopening and correction resolves the matter efficiently and avoids the need for further enforcement action.

## **1.8) Creditor Investigation Duties & Bank Liability**

Once a services-not-rendered dispute is supported by documentary evidence, the issuing bank is not permitted to rely solely on merchant rebuttal narratives that contradict the factual record.

Under **Regulation Z — 12 CFR §1026.13**, the creditor must:

• conduct a reasonable investigation  
• review submitted documentation in good faith  
• resolve disputes based on evidence  
• not shift the burden to the consumer once proof is submitted  
• acknowledge disputes within 30 days  
• resolve disputes within two billing cycles  

Repeated requests for documentation already submitted, followed by denial on a false “missing documentation” premise, is inconsistent with the creditor’s duty to perform a meaningful investigation.

A creditor may not close a billing error dispute based on procedural technicalities when the evidentiary record establishes non-delivery.

Failure to properly investigate exposes the creditor to liability under:

• Truth in Lending Act enforcement provisions  
• Regulation Z dispute handling obligations  
• Dodd-Frank UDAAP standards  
• unfair or deceptive practices by covered entities  
• CFPB supervisory expectations for reasonable investigations  

---

## **Mastercard Compliance Obligations**

Under Mastercard dispute processing rules, the issuing bank is required to:

• evaluate chargeback eligibility based on delivery of services  
• not elevate unsigned merchant terms above transaction evidence  
• treat non-delivery as a valid reason code event  
• prevent merchants from curing non-performance with token activity  

Where the merchant fails to deliver the contracted service, Mastercard standards require the dispute to proceed under:

**Reason Code 4853 — Goods or Services Not Provided**

Failure to properly process an eligible dispute is a network compliance issue, not a discretionary judgment call.

When a bank denies a dispute supported by documentary evidence of non-delivery, the issue is no longer a consumer complaint — it becomes a regulatory concern.

Regulators evaluate patterns of:

• improper dispute denials

• procedural closures without substantive review  

These patterns trigger supervisory review because they undermine the consumer protections embedded in federal credit law.

## **1.4.A Preparatory Activity Cannot Satisfy the Essential Purpose of the Contract**

The merchant may argue that access to analytics software or preliminary research constituted partial performance.

Even assuming analytics research is a preparatory component of the workflow, preparatory steps do not equal delivery of the contracted service.

The transaction was not for consulting, research assistance, or software access.

The transaction was for a Done-For-You Airbnb acquisition and deployment resulting in an operational, furnished, revenue-generating property.

Under contract law, performance is measured by fulfillment of the **essential purpose** of the agreement — not by isolated preparatory activity.

See:

• Restatement (Second) of Contracts §235  
• UCC failure of consideration principles  
• Texas contract law on essential purpose and material breach

The essential purpose required:

• acquisition of a landlord-approved property  
• furnishing and interior deployment  
• listing activation  
• operational launch  
• revenue generation capability  

None of these occurred.

Where the essential purpose of a contract fails, preparatory work cannot convert non-performance into performance.

Courts consistently reject the argument that incomplete preparation satisfies a contract whose central objective was never achieved.

At most, analytics access represents abandoned preliminary activity that never matured into delivery.

This is legally classified as:

• failure of consideration  
• material breach  
• services not rendered  
• unjust enrichment if payment is retained  

A party cannot retain full payment by pointing to incomplete preparation when the contracted result was never delivered.

That principle applies equally in contract law and card network dispute frameworks.

---

## **1.4.B Token Activity Cannot Cure Total Non-Delivery**

Providing temporary access to low-cost third-party software does not constitute delivery of a high-value DFY deployment system.

This is not partial fulfillment.

This is an attempt to manufacture the appearance of activity to defeat chargeback eligibility.

Mastercard dispute standards evaluate:

delivery of the contracted service  
not peripheral activity  
not unrelated tools  
not token gestures  

Under Mastercard Reason Code 4853 (Goods or Services Not Provided), the test is binary:

Was the promised service delivered as agreed?

Here:

no property was acquired  
no listing was launched  
no system was operational  
no revenue capability existed  

Therefore:

the contracted service was not delivered.

Token activity cannot substitute for contractual performance.

Allowing merchants to defeat disputes by pointing to trivial or unrelated activity would nullify consumer protection frameworks entirely.

Card network rules explicitly prevent this outcome.

---

## **1.4.C Retention of Payment After Non-Performance Creates Unjust Enrichment**

If a merchant retains full payment after failing to deliver the essential purpose of the contract, the legal consequence is unjust enrichment.

Unjust enrichment occurs when:

payment is received  
the bargained-for benefit is not delivered  
the recipient retains the money anyway  

Courts treat unjust enrichment as an equitable remedy independent of contract disputes.

Even absent formal contract analysis, equity requires restitution when performance fails.

This principle reinforces chargeback eligibility.

The consumer paid for a result.

The result does not exist.

Retention of funds under those circumstances is legally indefensible.

This submission concerns a billing dispute arising from a paid transaction for a Done-For-You Airbnb acquisition and deployment program that was never delivered.

# **SECTION 3 — Regulatory Exposure & Financial Liability**

### **3.1 Truth in Lending Act Exposure**

Under 15 U.S.C. §1640 (Truth in Lending Act civil liability), a creditor that fails to comply with billing dispute duties may be liable for:

- actual damages  
- statutory damages (up to $5,000 per violation in individual actions)  
- finance charge reimbursement  
- attorney’s fees  
- litigation costs  

Where a dispute is denied despite documentary evidence of non-delivery, exposure is not theoretical — it is statutory.

Courts routinely award fees that exceed the underlying transaction amount.

---

### **3.2 Finance Charge & Restitution Exposure**

If a billing error is improperly denied, the creditor may be required to:

- reverse the disputed amount  
- reverse related finance charges  
- reimburse fees  
- restore credit standing  
- compensate for wrongful collection activity  

Even a small dispute can produce disproportionate liability once fees and interest are added.

---

### **3.3 Dodd-Frank UDAAP Civil Penalty Exposure**

Under 12 U.S.C. §5565, federal regulators may impose civil money penalties for unfair or deceptive practices:

Tier 1: up to ~$7,000 per day  
Tier 2: up to ~$35,000 per day (reckless violation)  
Tier 3: up to ~$1,000,000 per day (knowing violation)

These figures apply to supervisory enforcement actions — not private lawsuits — but they illustrate the seriousness of procedural violations involving consumer credit disputes.

A documented pattern of improper investigation increases regulatory scrutiny.

- compliance assessments  
- dispute monitoring program placement  
- financial penalties  
- network audits  
- remediation mandates  

Card networks treat systemic dispute mishandling as a compliance risk, not a customer service issue.

Even a straightforward billing error lawsuit typically involves:

- attorney fees exceeding the transaction value  
- discovery costs  
- expert testimony  
- court expenses  
- settlement exposure  

No party benefits from converting a correctable dispute into litigation.

The evidentiary posture of this case favors restitution.

## **3.3.A — Escalation Risk When Conduct Becomes Reckless**

UDAAP penalty tiers escalate based on mental state.

The key pivot is:

> continuing a known improper practice after notice

Once a creditor is informed of procedural defects and continues the same handling, regulators evaluate that conduct under **reckless or knowing tiers**, not Tier 1.

In practical enforcement history:

- repeated denial after notice
- ignoring documentary evidence
- procedural closure without investigation

are classic triggers for Tier 2 review.

> Texas case law: T.O. Stanley Boot Co. v. Bank of El Paso, 847 S.W.2d 218 (Tex. 1992) - express terms (the
> invoice) govern; implied terms cannot override.
> Under well-established contract principles, including Restatement (Second) of Contracts §17 and UCC §2-207,
> terms provided after payment do not constitute mutual assent and cannot retroactively alter the bargain. Texas
> courts (see T.O. Stanley Boot Co. v. Bank of El Paso, 847 S.W.2d 218, and Midwest Builders v. Plano
> Development, 451 S.W.3d 714) have consistently held that unsigned, post-payment documents do not bind a
> consumer. Accordingly, the only enforceable instrument is the Invoice itself, which governs the scope and price
> of services.

# **SECTION 5 – Regulatory Notice, Non-Retaliation Protections, & Parallel Remedies**

## **5.1 Regulatory Notice (Good-Faith Disclosure)**

This submission is made in good faith with the intent to resolve this matter cooperatively and without unnecessary escalation.

However, where a federally regulated creditor:
- denies a supported billing error dispute,
- relies on unsigned merchant terms,
- deprives the consumer of meaningful notice,
- and closes the dispute through procedure rather than evidence,

federal law provides **parallel oversight mechanisms** independent of private litigation.

Accordingly, if this matter is not resolved promptly on the merits, I am prepared to submit formal complaints to appropriate oversight bodies, including:

- **Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)**  
  (Billing dispute handling, Reg Z compliance, UDAAP review)

- **Office of the Comptroller / Federal Reserve oversight channel**  
  (Depending on charter and supervisory authority)

- **State-level consumer protection regulators (Minnesota)**  
  (For unfair or deceptive practices affecting a Minnesota consumer)

This is not a threat.  
It is a factual statement of statutory rights and standard escalation pathways when dispute resolution fails.

---

## **5.2 ECOA Non-Retaliation & Anti-Discrimination Notice**

Federal law expressly prohibits retaliation or adverse action against a consumer for asserting protected rights.

Under the **Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA), 15 U.S.C. §1691**, and implementing Regulation B:

- A creditor may not discriminate against or penalize a consumer  
  for exercising rights under consumer credit protection laws.
- Adverse treatment linked to dispute activity, complaints, or enforcement efforts is prohibited.

Accordingly, I formally request and expect written confirmation that:

- This dispute and its resolution will **not be reported or characterized negatively**
- No adverse action, account limitation, repricing, or relationship impairment  
  will occur as a result of asserting my lawful dispute rights
- My standing and relationship with First Interstate Bank will remain intact

This request is consistent with ECOA, UDAAP principles, and CFPB supervisory expectations.

---

## **5.3 UDAAP Risk Clarification (Contextual, Not Accusatory)**

Under **Dodd-Frank’s UDAAP framework**, conduct may be deemed unfair when it:

- causes substantial consumer injury,
- is not reasonably avoidable by the consumer,
- and is not outweighed by countervailing benefits.

Requiring a traveling consumer to respond to physical mail only,  
while refusing digital delivery,  
despite confirmed knowledge of travel status,  
and then closing a dispute for “non-response,”

creates precisely the type of **avoidable consumer harm** UDAAP is designed to prevent.

This is especially true when the underlying transaction involves:
- documented non-delivery,
- partial refund admissions by the merchant,
- and reliance on unsigned post-payment terms.

I raise this not to accuse, but to underscore why prompt corrective action is the lowest-risk and most compliant outcome.

---

## **5.4 Settlement Preference Reaffirmed**

Despite the above, my preference remains resolution — not escalation.

If the dispute is corrected by:
- refunding the remaining **$10,500**
- reversing associated interest and fees
- addressing the documented consequential losses in good faith
- confirming non-retaliation and account integrity

then **no regulatory filings are necessary**.

Resolution at this stage benefits all parties and avoids unnecessary cost, scrutiny, and administrative burden.

## 2. Remaining Attack Vectors (and How to Eliminate Them)

Even weak opponents look for *something*. Here’s what they might try — and how to shut it down.

### Attack Vector 1:  
**“This is just a contractual dispute between consumer and merchant.”**

#### Neutralization (already mostly done, but can be sharpened):
You already framed this as:
- **Services not rendered**
- **Fraudulent inducement**
- **Bank procedural failure**

**Upgrade recommendation (small but powerful):**
Add one sentence (plain English + legal):

> “This dispute does not arise from a disagreement over performance quality or business outcomes. It arises from the total absence of the contracted service itself, combined with the creditor’s failure to follow mandatory billing-error investigation procedures.”

This reframes it as **statutory**, not contractual.

---

### Attack Vector 2:  
**“The merchant provided something (AirDNA / research).”**

You already crushed this — but we can make it nuclear.

#### Upgrade:
Add a **one-line value comparison**:

> “The merchant’s claimed ‘performance’ consists of temporary access to a third-party tool retailing for approximately $34–$125/month, offered in place of a $18,000 DFY acquisition service. This does not constitute partial performance under any reasonable commercial standard.”

This makes the argument **economically absurd**, not just legally wrong.

### Attack Vector 3:  
**“The chargeback is outside network timelines.”**

This is the bank’s weakest point — and also where you win hardest.

- Notice failure
- Travel knowledge
- Mail-only delivery
- Repeated requests for digital copies
- No actual receipt

That word — **estopped** — matters.

### Attack Vector 4:

### 📍 **PASTE THIS AT THE END OF SECTION 2.4 (Procedural Impact)**

### 2.4.A) Equitable Estoppel of Timeline Defenses

A creditor may not rely on procedural timelines where its own conduct prevented the consumer from receiving notice or responding.

Here, First Interstate Bank:
- relied exclusively on physical mail despite repeated requests for digital delivery,
- continued physical-mail-only correspondence while having confirmed knowledge the consumer was traveling,
- failed to ensure actual receipt of dispute communications,
- and closed the dispute based on an alleged non-response to a letter the consumer never received.

Under principles of equitable estoppel, a party may not benefit from deadlines it caused the opposing party to miss. Where notice is defective, timelines are tolled as a matter of law.

Accordingly, any claim that this dispute is “outside chargeback timelines” is legally barred by the bank’s own notice failures.

	 • the issued invoice documenting a fixed-fee DFY acquisition program

This establishes:
clear inducement terms
performance expectations
reliance


1.3) Verified Outcome After Eleven Weeks

After more than eleven weeks from payment:

 	 • no property was acquired
	 • no lease was secured
	 • no furnishing occurred
	 • no design work was completed
	 • no photography was scheduled
	 • no listing went live

	 • no revenue was generated
	 • no DFY system was deployed
	 • no promised deliverable was fulfilled

This is not partial performance.
This is total non-delivery of the core service purchased.


1.4) Merchant’s Post-Payment Defense

The merchant later attempted to justify non-delivery by:
introducing unsigned, post-payment “terms” 
asserting retroactive hourly billing 
presenting rules never disclosed
presenting documents never agreed to
presenting documents never signed

The merchant also attempts to characterize delivery as:
temporary access to shared AIRDNA software costing approximately $34-$125/month

This software access:
 	 • expired after 3-4 weeks
	 • is a low-cost third-party tool
	 • provides inaccurate data
	 • has trivial commercial value
	 • does not replace the contracted service

This is not performance.
This is an attempt to manufacture the appearance of activity to defeat a chargeback.


1.4.A) Preparatory Activity Cannot Satisfy the Essential Purpose of the Contract
The merchant may argue that access to analytics software or preliminary research constituted partial performance.

Even assuming analytics research is a preparatory component of the workflow, preparatory steps do not equal delivery of the contracted service
.
The transaction was not for consulting, research assistance, or software access.
The transaction was for a Done-For-You Airbnb acquisition and deployment resulting in an operational, furnished, revenue-generating property.

Under contract law, performance is measured by fulfillment of the essential purpose of the agreement - not by isolated preparatory activity.

See:
 	 • Restatement (Second) of Contracts §235
	 • UCC failure of consideration principles
	 • Texas contract law on essential purpose and material breach

The essential purpose required:

 • acquisition of a landlord-approved property
	 • furnishing and interior deployment
	 • listing activation
	 • operational launch
	 • revenue generation capability

None of these occurred.

Where the essential purpose of a contract fails, preparatory work cannot convert non-performance into performance.

Courts consistently reject the argument that incomplete preparation satisfies a contract whose central objective was never achieved.
At most, analytics access represents abandoned preliminary activity that never matured into delivery.

This is legally classified as:

 • failure of consideration
	 • material breach
	 • services not rendered
	 • unjust enrichment if payment is retained

A party cannot retain full payment by pointing to incomplete preparation when the contracted result was never delivered.

That principle applies equally in contract law and card network dispute frameworks.


1.4.B) Token Activity Cannot Cure Total Non-Delivery

Providing temporary access to low-cost third-party software does not constitute delivery of a high-value DFY deployment system.

This is not partial fulfillment.
This is an attempt to manufacture the appearance of activity to defeat chargeback eligibility.

Mastercard dispute standards evaluate:
delivery of the contracted service
not peripheral activity
not unrelated tools
not token gestures

Under Mastercard Reason Code 4853 (Goods or Services Not Provided), the test is binary:

Was the promised service delivered as agreed?
Here:
no property was acquired
no listing was launched
no system was operational
no revenue capability existed

Therefore:
the contracted service was not delivered.

Token activity cannot substitute for contractual performance.

Allowing merchants to defeat disputes by pointing to trivial or unrelated activity would nullify consumer protection frameworks entirely.
Card network rules explicitly prevent this outcome.


1.4.C) Retention of Payment After Non-Performance Creates Unjust Enrichment
If a merchant retains full payment after failing to deliver the essential purpose of the contract, the legal consequence is unjust enrichment.
Unjust enrichment occurs when:
payment is received
the bargained-for benefit is not delivered
the recipient retains the money anyway

Courts treat unjust enrichment as an equitable remedy independent of contract disputes.

Even absent formal contract analysis, equity requires restitution when performance fails.
This principle reinforces chargeback eligibility.
The consumer paid for a result.
The result does not exist.
Retention of funds under those circumstances is legally indefensible.


1.5) Legal Characterization of Merchant Conduct

Post-payment contract fabrication cannot cure non-performance.
Token software access cannot substitute for a DFY business deployment.

This conduct independently constitutes deceptive practice under:

 	 • FTC Act §5 - unfair or deceptive acts
	 • Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act §17.46
	 • failure of consideration doctrine
	 • common law fraudulent inducement principles

The essential purpose of the contract was never performed.

Under contract law:
trivial acts do not satisfy primary obligations


1.6) Legal Classification of the Dispute

This dispute is a textbook case of:

 	 • Goods/Services Not Provided
	 • Failure of Consideration
	 • Misrepresentation
	 • Fraudulent Inducement
 	 • Unenforceable Post-Payment Contract Attempt

Under Mastercard Reason Code 4853
 (Goods or Services Not Provided)
chargeback eligibility is established when promised services are not delivered.

The merchant’s attempt to rewrite the agreement after payment does not eliminate original non-delivery.


1.6.A) KEY LEGAL POINT: Unenforceable Post-Payment Terms

A contract requires mutual assent.

The merchant has produced no signed agreement, no acceptance record, and no contemporaneous disclosure showing that the consumer agreed to the “terms” now being asserted.

Terms introduced after payment - or never disclosed at all - are legally unenforceable and cannot be used to:

justify non-delivery
convert non-performance into performance
defeat consumer protection rights


Treating unilateral, unsigned merchant assertions as binding terms contradicts basic contract law principles and cannot support a valid dispute denial.

Additionally, even if a merchant claims “terms exist,” the operative question is whether there is evidence of mutual assent at or before payment (signature, clickwrap acceptance record, or contemporaneous disclosure tied to the transaction). 

The merchant has provided no enforceable acceptance record for the post-payment terms now being asserted. Therefore, those terms cannot defeat a services-not-rendered claim or convert non-performance into performance.



1.7) Binary Record of the Case

The record is legally binary when evaluated against the contracted service.
A promised Done-For-You Airbnb deployment service exists
Payment for that service exists
The contracted service was never performed


No property was acquired.
No Airbnb was launched.
No DFY system was deployed.

Any unrelated third-party software access referenced by the merchant does not constitute delivery of the contracted service and has no bearing on performance analysis.

Under contract law, performance is measured by fulfillment of the essential purpose of the agreement. That essential purpose was never achieved.
This satisfies the legal definition of: Services Not Rendered.



1.8) Creditor Investigation Duties & Bank Liability

Once a services-not-rendered dispute is supported by documentary evidence, the issuing bank is not permitted to rely solely on merchant rebuttal narratives that contradict the factual record.

Under Regulation Z - 12 CFR §1026.13, the creditor must:

 	 • conduct a reasonable investigation
	 • review submitted documentation in good faith
	 • resolve disputes based on evidence
	 • not shift the burden to the consumer once proof is submitted
	 • acknowledge disputes within 30 days
	 • resolve disputes within two billing cycles

Repeated requests for documentation already submitted, followed by denial on a false “missing documentation” premise, is inconsistent with the creditor’s duty to perform a meaningful investigation.

A creditor may not close a billing error dispute based on procedural technicalities when the evidentiary record establishes non-delivery.

Failure to properly investigate exposes the creditor to liability under:

 • Truth in Lending Act enforcement provisions
 • Regulation Z dispute handling obligations
 • Dodd-Frank UDAAP standards
 • unfair or deceptive practices by covered entities
 • CFPB supervisory expectations for reasonable investigations


1.9) Procedural Timeline Violations & Denial of Meaningful Notice

This dispute was not denied on the merits.
It was denied through a procedural structure that deprived the consumer of a meaningful opportunity to respond.
